Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Browser drops Minecraft-client-themed JAR to user Downloads
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] javaw.exe / java.exe executes JAR from user Downloads or .minecraft folder
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] WeedHack MaaS C2 beacon to receiver.cy / whreceive.ru / 45.141.119.34 · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Java process reads browser / Discord / Telegram / Minecraft credential stores · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
[LLM] WeedHack MaaS C2 beacon to receiver.cy / whreceive.ru / 45.141.119.34 Command & Control High
Detects any endpoint reaching the named WeedHack receiver infrastructure (clear-net MaaS dashboard hosts and remote-shell relay). Because these domains/IP only serve trojanized Minecraft client traffic, a single hit is high-fidelity evidence of infection. Rationale: Uses the seven C2 domains and the 45.141.119.34 receiver IP enumerated verbatim in the McAfee report and the article's IOC block. These hosts have no legitimate use, so equality match is sufficient. No external corroboration searched – IOCs were taken directly from the article and the prompt's pre-extracted IOC list.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1219 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
let WeedHackDomains = dynamic(["receiver.cy","weedhack.cy","whreceive.ru","whreceiver.ru","marsalek.cy","huehnchenfarm.ru","remotev2.whreceive.ru"]);
let WeedHackIPs = dynamic(["45.141.119.34"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (WeedHackIPs)
   or RemoteUrl has_any (WeedHackDomains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc

  (CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DestinationIP in (WeedHackIPs) or DestinationHostName in~ (WeedHackDomains) or RequestURL has_any (WeedHackDomains) | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceVendor)

[LLM] Browser drops Minecraft-client-themed JAR to user Downloads Delivery Medium
Detects when a browser writes a .jar file whose name matches the WeedHack-impersonated client families (Meteor, Wurst, LiquidBounce, Skytils, Impact, Aristois, Future, Inertia, Cornos, WWE, 3arthh4ck, Salhack, Phobos, Gamesense, Radium). Pairs the file write with the originating download URL so the SEO-poisoned / YouTube-linked distribution site can be triaged. Rationale: The client list (Meteor, Radium, Wurst, Aristois, LiquidBounce, Impact, Future, Inertia, Cornos, WWE, 3arthh4ck, Salhack, Phobos, Gamesense) is enumerated verbatim in the article. Combining that with a browser parent and a .jar extension turns a generic 'JAR downloaded' signal into article-specific intent. FileOriginUrl/FileOriginReferrerUrl in Defender additionally captures the SEO-poisoned site or YouTube-linked CDN for downstream blocking.
ATT&CKT1189 T1566.002 T1608.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
let ClientKeywords = dynamic(["meteor","wurst","liquidbounce","skytils","impact","aristois","future","inertia","cornos","3arthh4ck","salhack","phobos","gamesense","radium","wwe"]);
let Browsers = dynamic(["chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","opera_gx.exe","vivaldi.exe"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".jar"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (Browsers)
| where tolower(FileName) has_any (ClientKeywords)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginReferrerUrl, FileOriginIP, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let ClientKeywords = dynamic(["meteor","wurst","liquidbounce","skytils","impact","aristois","future","inertia","cornos","3arthh4ck","salhack","phobos","gamesense","radium","wwe"]);
let Browsers = dynamic(["chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileExtension =~ "jar"
| where ActingProcessName has_any (Browsers)
| where tolower(TargetFileName) has_any (ClientKeywords)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256

[LLM] javaw.exe / java.exe executes JAR from user Downloads or .minecraft folder Exploitation Medium
Detects the Java runtime spawning to execute a .jar file located in the user's Downloads directory or under %APPDATA%\.minecraft, the exact execution shape McAfee describes for WeedHack victim infection. Combined with a recent file-write window this is a tight execution-stage pivot. Rationale: Article explicitly states 'javaw.exe / java.exe child processes spawned from user Downloads or %APPDATA%\.minecraft directories' as the execution shape. The path constraints turn an otherwise noisy java.exe execution into article-specific intent: the legitimate Minecraft launcher loads JARs from versions\<v>\ and libraries\, never from Downloads or root .minecraft.
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".jar"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Desktop\", @"\AppData\Roaming\.minecraft\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MinecraftLauncher.exe","javaws.exe","MicrosoftStore.exe","explorer.exe") or InitiatingProcessFileName == "explorer.exe"  // surface explorer-launched JARs (user double-click) but flag for review
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\java.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\javaw.exe"
| where CommandLine has ".jar"
| where CommandLine has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Desktop\", @"\AppData\Roaming\.minecraft\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Java Executes JAR From Downloads or .minecraft Folder (WeedHack)
id: 9e1f17d7-95cc-4f8a-94f7-9b2b0a1d1d4e
description: Detects javaw.exe or java.exe invoked against a .jar in a user-writable location (Downloads, Desktop, %APPDATA%\.minecraft), the WeedHack victim-execution shape.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/over-116-000-mincraft-systems-infected-in-weedhack-malware-campaign/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/03
tags:

  - attack.t1204.002
  - attack.t1059.006
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_image:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\java.exe'
      - '\javaw.exe'
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '.jar'
  selection_path:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '\Downloads\'
      - '\Desktop\'
      - '\AppData\Roaming\.minecraft\'
      - '\AppData\Local\Temp\'
  condition: selection_image and selection_cmd and selection_path
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon AND @EventID:1 AND @Image:(*\java.exe OR *\javaw.exe OR *\Java.exe OR *\Javaw.exe) AND @CommandLine:(*.jar* OR *.JAR*) AND @CommandLine:(*\\Downloads\\* OR *\\downloads\\* OR *\\Desktop\\* OR *\\AppData\\Roaming\\.minecraft\\* OR *\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\javaw?\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)\\.jar", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(?i)\\\\(Downloads|Desktop|AppData\\\\Roaming\\\\\\.minecraft|AppData\\\\Local\\\\Temp)\\\\", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())

[LLM] Java process reads browser / Discord / Telegram / Minecraft credential stores Actions on Objectives High
Detects java.exe or javaw.exe touching the canonical credential and session-token files harvested by WeedHack's free-tier stealer: Chromium 'Login Data' / 'Cookies' / 'Local State', Firefox profiles, Discord leveldb, Telegram tdata, Steam loginusers.vdf, and .minecraft\launcher_accounts.json. Rationale: WeedHack's free-tier capabilities are listed verbatim in the article: 'cookies, and saved passwords across 36 browsers, 56 cryptocurrency add-ons, 12 desktop cryptocurrency wallet apps, Discord, Steam, and Telegram credentials'. The detection pivots on the canonical on-disk locations of those stores being touched specifically by the Java runtime, which is unique to a JAR-delivered stealer. The HitCount >= 2 guard removes single coincidental reads (e.g. Minecraft launcher legitimately reading launcher_accounts.json) while keeping the multi-store harvest signal. Sigma omitted because the >=2-distinct-stores threshold is a count correlation, not single-event-shape.
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
let CredentialPaths = dynamic([
  @"\User Data\", 
  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\",
  @"\discord\Local Storage\leveldb\",
  @"\Telegram Desktop\tdata\",
  @"\Steam\config\loginusers.vdf",
  @"\Steam\ssfn",
  @"\.minecraft\launcher_accounts.json",
  @"\.minecraft\launcher_profiles.json"
]);
let CredentialFiles = dynamic(["Login Data","Cookies","Local State","key4.db","logins.json","loginusers.vdf","launcher_accounts.json","launcher_profiles.json"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
| where (FolderPath has_any (CredentialPaths)) or (FileName in~ (CredentialFiles))
| summarize HitCount = count(), FilesTouched = make_set(FolderPath, 50), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| where HitCount >= 2   // 2 = touching at least two distinct credential stores rules out a single coincidental read
| order by LastSeen desc
let CredentialPaths = dynamic([@"\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\", @"\discord\Local Storage\leveldb\", @"\Telegram Desktop\tdata\", @"\Steam\config\loginusers.vdf", @"\Steam\ssfn", @"\.minecraft\launcher_accounts.json"]);
let CredentialFiles = dynamic(["Login Data","Cookies","Local State","key4.db","logins.json","loginusers.vdf","launcher_accounts.json"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
| where (TargetFilePath has_any (CredentialPaths)) or (TargetFileName in~ (CredentialFiles))
| summarize HitCount = count(), FilesTouched = make_set(TargetFilePath, 50), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessId, ActingProcessCommandLine
| where HitCount >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon AND @EventID:11 AND @Image:(*\java.exe OR *\javaw.exe OR *\Java.exe OR *\Javaw.exe) AND @TargetFilename:(*\\User\ Data\\*\\Login\ Data* OR *\\User\ Data\\*\\Cookies* OR *\\User\ Data\\Local\ State* OR *\\Mozilla\\Firefox\\Profiles\\*key4.db OR *\\Mozilla\\Firefox\\Profiles\\*logins.json OR *\\discord\\Local\ Storage\\leveldb\\* OR *\\Telegram\ Desktop\\tdata\\* OR *\\Steam\\config\\loginusers.vdf OR *\\Steam\\ssfn* OR *\\.minecraft\\launcher_accounts.json OR *\\.minecraft\\launcher_profiles.json)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo ContextImageFileName=/\\javaw?\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)(\\\\User Data\\\\.*\\\\(Login Data|Cookies|Local State)|\\\\Mozilla\\\\Firefox\\\\Profiles\\\\.*\\\\(key4\\.db|logins\\.json)|\\\\discord\\\\Local Storage\\\\leveldb\\\\|\\\\Telegram Desktop\\\\tdata\\\\|\\\\Steam\\\\(config\\\\loginusers\\.vdf|ssfn)|\\\\\\.minecraft\\\\launcher_(accounts|profiles)\\.json)", field=TargetFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ContextImageFileName], function={ count() | targets := collect([TargetFileName]) })
| _count > 1
ENDPOINT

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

AI-built ransomware toolkit automates EDR evasion, AD discovery

BleepingComputer
2026-06-02 7 use cases 2 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

A threat actor is using an AI-built ransomware attack toolkit that automates Active Directory discovery and helps evade endpoint detection and response (EDR) solutions. [...]

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Payload staging in user 'Documents\test' folder — AI-built ransomware toolkit drop path
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Telegram Bot API C2 channel used by AI-built ransomware toolkit (non-IM/non-browser egress) · [LLM] First-time egress to *.workers.dev (Cloudflare Worker C2 redirector) from non-browser process · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
[LLM] Telegram Bot API C2 channel used by AI-built ransomware toolkit (non-IM/non-browser egress) Command & Control High
Hunts for processes other than known browsers and Telegram desktop clients reaching api.telegram.org — the toolkit Sophos analysed routes beacon traffic through the Telegram Bot API instead of direct C2. Custom Rust/Go loaders and curl/PowerShell wrappers are the typical callers in this campaign. Rationale: Targets the article's explicit 'Telegram bot API-based external C2 mechanism that routed communication through Telegram's infrastructure rather than using direct connections.' Tightens the existing generic Sigma (detection.fyi) by also flagging unsigned/non-IM-vendor process metadata characteristic of Rust/Go beacons the toolkit produces. Cross-checked Sophos's own blog post and Splunk Security Content's 'Windows DNS Query Request by Telegram Bot API' rule for non-duplication. Cross-checked against: • https://news.sophos.com/en-us/2026/06/02/ai-built-ransomware-toolkit/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/02/ai-agents-edr-evasion-techniques/ • https://detection.fyi/sigmahq/sigma/network/dns/net_dns_susp_telegram_api/ • https://research.splunk.com/network/86f66f44-94d9-412d-a71d-5d8ed0fef72e/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Resolution
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "api.telegram.org" or RemoteUrl matches regex @"(?i)api\.telegram\.org/bot[A-Za-z0-9:_\-]+"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("telegram.exe","telegramdesktop.exe","updater.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe","slack.exe","discord.exe","teams.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where isempty(InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName)
   or InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !in~ ("Microsoft Corporation","Google LLC","Mozilla Corporation","Telegram Messenger LLP","Slack Technologies, Inc.","Discord Inc.")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName,
          InitiatingProcessVersionInfoProductName,
          RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by Timestamp desc
let TelegramHosts = dynamic(["api.telegram.org"]);
let KnownIM = dynamic(["telegram.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","slack.exe","discord.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe","teams.exe"]);
let CmdlineHits = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where CommandLine has "api.telegram.org"
    | extend ProcName = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
    | where ProcName !in (KnownIM)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account=SubjectUserName, ProcessName=NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, Src="ProcessCmdLine";
let DnsHits = DnsEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Name =~ "api.telegram.org"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, Src="DNS";
union CmdlineHits, DnsHits
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Non-Browser Network Connection to Telegram Bot API (AI-built Ransomware Toolkit C2)
id: 7d9c8e2f-3b41-4a16-9e8c-2f1d7b4a9c01
status: experimental
description: Detects DNS resolution of api.telegram.org from processes other than known browsers/Telegram desktop, indicative of the AI-built ransomware toolkit's Telegram Bot API C2 (Sophos, 2026-06-02).
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/ai-built-ransomware-toolkit-automates-edr-evasion-ad-discovery/
  - https://news.sophos.com/en-us/2026/06/02/ai-built-ransomware-toolkit/
author: SOC Detection Eng
date: 2026/06/02
tags:
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.t1102
  - attack.command_and_control
logsource:
  category: dns
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    QueryName|endswith: 'api.telegram.org'
  filter_browsers:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
      - '\firefox.exe'
      - '\brave.exe'
      - '\opera.exe'
      - '\iexplore.exe'
      - '\telegram.exe'
      - '\telegramdesktop.exe'
      - '\updater.exe'
      - '\slack.exe'
      - '\discord.exe'
      - '\teams.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_browsers
falsepositives:
  - Internal chatops/monitoring bots using Telegram for alerting
  - Approved red-team engagements
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:22 @QueryName:api.telegram.org -@Image:(*\\telegram.exe OR *\\Telegram.exe OR *\\TELEGRAM.EXE OR *\\chrome.exe OR *\\Chrome.exe OR *\\msedge.exe OR *\\firefox.exe OR *\\Firefox.exe OR *\\brave.exe OR *\\slack.exe OR *\\Slack.exe OR *\\discord.exe OR *\\Discord.exe OR *\\teams.exe OR *\\Teams.exe OR *\\opera.exe OR *\\iexplore.exe)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/^api\.telegram\.org$/i
| ContextImageFileName!=/\\(chrome|msedge|firefox|brave|opera|iexplore|telegram|telegramdesktop|updater|slack|discord|teams)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count(as=Hits))
| Hits > 0
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmd values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent values(Processes.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*api.telegram.org*" OR Processes.process="*api.telegram.org/bot*") by Processes.dest Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where NOT match(process_name, "(?i)^(chrome|msedge|firefox|telegram|brave|slack|discord|opera|iexplore|teams)\.exe$") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmd values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent values(Processes.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*api.telegram.org*" OR Processes.process="*api.telegram.org/bot*") by Processes.dest Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where NOT match(process_name, "(?i)^(chrome|msedge|firefox|telegram|brave|slack|discord|opera|iexplore|teams)\.exe$") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
[LLM] First-time egress to *.workers.dev (Cloudflare Worker C2 redirector) from non-browser process Command & Control Medium
Detects a host reaching a Cloudflare Worker URL that has not been observed in the prior 30-day baseline, when the caller is not a sanctioned browser. The Sophos toolkit specifically uses a Cloudflare Worker as a front-end redirector to obscure the actual backend C2 server. Rationale: Targets the article's call-out that the toolkit deploys 'A Cloudflare Worker acting as a front-end redirector to obscure the actual backend C2 server.' Anti-pattern guidance in the house style says don't blanket-allow workers.dev — instead flag the first-time-per-host. Pairs with UC1 (Telegram) — same host hitting both is a confirmed-bad signal. Cross-checked against hunt.io's 'Russian-Speaking Threat Actor Abuses Cloudflare & Telegram' write-up showing the same TTP combination. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/russian-actor-cloudflare-phishing-telegram-c2 • https://news.sophos.com/en-us/2026/06/02/ai-built-ransomware-toolkit/
ATT&CKT1090.002 T1102.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb Network_Traffic Network_Resolution
let Lookback = 30d;
let Recent = 1h;
let Known = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(Lookback) .. ago(Recent))
    | where RemoteUrl endswith ".workers.dev"
    | summarize by RemoteUrl;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(Recent)
| where RemoteUrl endswith ".workers.dev"
| join kind=leftanti Known on RemoteUrl
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe","slack.exe","teams.exe","outlook.exe","webex.exe","safari.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName,
          RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let Lookback = 30d;
let Recent = 1h;
let Known = DnsEvents
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(Lookback) .. ago(Recent))
    | where Name endswith ".workers.dev"
    | summarize by Name;
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Recent)
| where Name endswith ".workers.dev"
| join kind=leftanti Known on Name
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), QueryCount=count(), HostCount=dcount(Computer), ClientIPs=make_set(ClientIP, 25) by Name
| order by FirstSeen desc

[LLM] Payload staging in user 'Documents\test' folder — AI-built ransomware toolkit drop path Installation High
Detects executable, DLL, or script files being written to '\Users\<user>\Documents\test\' — the exact staging directory Sophos observed in the victim environment for this toolkit's Cobalt Strike profiles, Python loaders, and shellcode-injection scripts. Catches operator-driven file drops before payload execution. Rationale: Pivots on the exact victim-side staging path Sophos disclosed: 'payloads stored in C:\Users\User\Documents\test'. Generalised to any user profile (any '\Users\<x>\Documents\test\') to catch the operator's standard drop pattern across hosts in the same environment. Extension filter targets the languages/file types Sophos enumerated (Python, Rust, Go, Cobalt Strike DLLs). Cross-checked against: • https://news.sophos.com/en-us/2026/06/02/ai-built-ransomware-toolkit/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/02/ai-agents-edr-evasion-techniques/
ATT&CKT1105 T1074.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)\\Users\\[^\\]+\\Documents\\test\\"
| where FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName endswith ".dll" or FileName endswith ".ps1"
   or FileName endswith ".py"  or FileName endswith ".bat" or FileName endswith ".cmd"
   or FileName endswith ".js"  or FileName endswith ".vbs" or FileName endswith ".hta"
   or FileName endswith ".rs"  or FileName endswith ".go"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, FileSize
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath matches regex @"(?i)\\Users\\[^\\]+\\Documents\\test\\"
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("exe","dll","ps1","py","bat","cmd","js","vbs","hta","rs","go")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, TargetFileSize
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Payload Staging in User Documents\test Folder (AI-built Ransomware Toolkit)
id: 8b4f5d10-9c72-4d1a-83fa-7a6c1f0b5d12
status: experimental
description: Detects executable/DLL/script files being written to a 'Documents\test\' subdirectory under any user profile — the exact staging path Sophos observed for the AI-built ransomware toolkit's payloads (Cobalt Strike profiles, Python injectors, Rust/Go beacons).
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/ai-built-ransomware-toolkit-automates-edr-evasion-ad-discovery/
  - https://news.sophos.com/en-us/2026/06/02/ai-built-ransomware-toolkit/
author: SOC Detection Eng
date: 2026/06/02
tags:
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.t1074.001
  - attack.command_and_control
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\Documents\test\'
      - '\Documents\Test\'
      - '\Documents\TEST\'
  selection_ext:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '.exe'
      - '.dll'
      - '.ps1'
      - '.py'
      - '.bat'
      - '.cmd'
      - '.js'
      - '.vbs'
      - '.hta'
  condition: selection_path and selection_ext
falsepositives:
  - Developer storing test binaries under a personal Documents\test folder
  - QA engineer compiling test artefacts to this location
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\Documents\\test\\* OR *\\Documents\\Test\\* OR *\\Documents\\TEST\\*) @TargetFilename:(*.exe OR *.dll OR *.ps1 OR *.py OR *.bat OR *.cmd OR *.js OR *.vbs OR *.hta)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\\Users\\[^\\]+\\Documents\\test\\/i
| TargetFileName=/\.(exe|dll|ps1|py|bat|cmd|js|vbs|hta|rs|go)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count(as=Writes))
| Writes > 0
ENDPOINT

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_path) as paths values(Filesystem.process_name) as proc values(Filesystem.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_path="*\\Users\\*\\Documents\\test\\*" (Filesystem.file_name="*.exe" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.dll" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.ps1" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.py" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.bat" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.cmd" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.js" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.vbs" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.hta") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents

| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName

| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

            - '\wscript.exe'

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")

AuditLogs

         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gamaredon Exploits WinRAR to Deliver GammaWorm and GammaSteel Against Ukraine

The Hacker News
2026-06-02 19 use cases 8 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

The Russian hacking group known as Gamaredon has been attributed to the continued exploitation of a WinRAR vulnerability to deliver multiple malware families aimed at data theft and propagation. Per Sekoia, the activity involves the weaponization of CVE-2025-8088, a path traversal flaw in WinRAR, to launch an HTML Application payload dubbed GammaPhish, which is then used to retrieve an

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 path traversal — file written from WinRAR into Startup folder · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] GammaPhish HTA auto-execution — mshta.exe launching from user Startup folder · [LLM] GammaWorm NTFS Alternate Data Stream module hide — script-host writes file with ADS suffix · [LLM] GammaSteel registry-staged module fan-out — PowerShell writes many binary blobs under one key · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] GammaWorm Telegram/Telegraph/Teletype/Cloudflare-Workers DDR resolution via curl from script host · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] GammaWorm USB / network-share propagation — script process mass-creates LNK files on removable or remote drives · [LLM] GammaSteel S3 exfiltration — script/PowerShell HTTP egress to AWS S3 bucket · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
[LLM] WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 path traversal — file written from WinRAR into Startup folder Delivery High
Hunts the GammaPhish initial-access signature: a WinRAR / UnRAR / RAR process writes a file into a Windows Startup directory. CVE-2025-8088 lets a malicious archive traverse out of the chosen extraction path; Gamaredon weaponises it to drop an HTA dropper that auto-runs at next logon. Rationale: Article + Sekoia explicitly state the WinRAR exploit drops an HTA into the Startup directory via path traversal. Pairing the archive-tool image with the Startup destination is the cleanest single-event signature for CVE-2025-8088 exploitation. Cross-checked Sekoia blog and follow-on Hacker News CVE-2025-8088 coverage. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/fsbs-matryoshka-1-3-gamaredons-gifts-that-keeps-unpacking-gammaphish-and-gammaworm/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/01/google-warns-of-active-exploitation-of.html • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/gamaredon-worm-ntfs-data-streams/
ATT&CKT1203 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winrar.exe","unrar.exe","rar.exe") | where FolderPath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\" | where FileName !endswith ".log" and FileName !endswith ".tmp" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, ArchiveTool=InitiatingProcessFileName, ArchiveCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, DroppedFile=FileName, DropPath=FolderPath, SHA256 | order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where ActingProcessName has_any ("winrar.exe","unrar.exe","rar.exe") | where TargetFilePath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\" | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256 | order by TimeGenerated desc
title: WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 Path Traversal Write Into Startup Folder

description: WinRAR / UnRAR / RAR process writes a file directly into a Windows Startup directory — indicative of CVE-2025-8088 path-traversal exploitation used by Gamaredon to drop GammaPhish HTA.

[LLM] GammaPhish HTA auto-execution — mshta.exe launching from user Startup folder Installation High
Hunts the GammaPhish auto-run: at next logon, explorer.exe launches mshta.exe against an HTA that CVE-2025-8088 dropped into the Startup folder. Pairing the parent (explorer) with the binary (mshta) and the HTA's path (Startup) is a high-fidelity catch for the post-exploit handoff to GammaLoad. Rationale: Sekoia and Hacker News articles describe the GammaPhish HTA being dropped directly into the Startup folder by the WinRAR exploit, which then auto-launches via mshta at logon. Combining explorer→mshta parentage with the Startup path eliminates the bulk of mshta noise from legitimate HTAs hosted elsewhere. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/fsbs-matryoshka-1-3-gamaredons-gifts-that-keeps-unpacking-gammaphish-and-gammaworm/ • https://cyberpress.org/gamaredon-apt-hides-malware/

SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where EventID == 4688 | where NewProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe" | where ParentProcessName endswith "\\explorer.exe" | where CommandLine has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\" | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine | order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] GammaWorm Telegram/Telegraph/Teletype/Cloudflare-Workers DDR resolution via curl from script host Command & Control High
Hunts the GammaWorm dead-drop-resolver step: a VBScript host (wscript / cscript / mshta) spawns curl.exe to fetch a hardcoded public Telegram channel page (t.me/telegra.ph) or its Teletype.in / Cloudflare Workers fall-back, from which the actual C2 address is parsed. Catches the exact platform abuse Sekoia documents. Rationale: Sekoia's report explicitly names Telegram, Telegra.ph, Teletype.in, and Cloudflare Workers as Gamaredon's DDR platforms, and curl as the GammaWorm fetch tool. Pairing curl with a script-host parent and one of these four domains is single-event-shape and very rare in a legit corporate environment. One of the article IOCs (bold.zsjtn41091.workers.dev) is a Cloudflare Workers DDR endpoint. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/fsbs-matryoshka-1-3-gamaredons-gifts-that-keeps-unpacking-gammaphish-and-gammaworm/ • https://cyberpress.org/gamaredon-apt-hides-malware/

[LLM] GammaWorm USB / network-share propagation — script process mass-creates LNK files on removable or remote drives Actions on Objectives High
Hunts GammaWorm's lateral-movement pattern: a VBScript host (wscript / cscript) writes many .lnk files to a removable drive or network share within a short window, while concurrently setting the hidden attribute on existing directories. The shortcut-replacing technique is Gamaredon's documented spread vector for USB and SMB. Rationale: Article specifies GammaWorm 'hide legitimate directories in network shares and USB drives and replace with malicious Windows Shortcut (LNK) files.' Detection keys on script-host parentage + drive letter outside C: or UNC root + LNK extension + burst count — none of these alone are unusual, but the combination is. Skipped Sigma because the threshold/grouping is multi-event correlation. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/fsbs-matryoshka-1-3-gamaredons-gifts-that-keeps-unpacking-gammaphish-and-gammaworm/ • https://cyberpress.org/gamaredon-apt-hides-malware/
ATT&CKT1091 T1080 T1547.009
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where ActionType == "FileCreated" | where FileName endswith ".lnk" | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe") | where FolderPath matches regex @"^(\\\\[^\\]+\\|[D-Z]:\\)" | summarize LnkCount=dcount(FileName), Samples=make_set(FileName, 5), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, bin(Timestamp, 10m) | where LnkCount >= 5
ImFileEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where EventType == "FileCreated" | where TargetFileName endswith ".lnk" | where ActingProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe") | where TargetFilePath matches regex @"^(\\\\[^\\]+\\|[D-Z]:\\)" | summarize LnkCount=dcount(TargetFileName), Samples=make_set(TargetFileName, 5) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m) | where LnkCount >= 5
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@Image:(*\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\WScript.exe OR *\\CScript.exe)) (@TargetFilename:(*.lnk OR *.LNK)) (@TargetFilename:(\\\\* OR D\:\\* OR E\:\\* OR F\:\\* OR G\:\\*))

[LLM] GammaWorm NTFS Alternate Data Stream module hide — script-host writes file with ADS suffix Installation Medium
Hunts the GammaWorm defence-evasion technique: a VBScript host writes one of its core modules into an Alternate Data Stream (filename:streamname pattern) on a host file. Sekoia documents this as the primary on-disk hiding mechanism for the worm's modules. Rationale: Article + Infosecurity Magazine + Sekoia all confirm GammaWorm uses NTFS Alternate Data Streams to conceal its core modules. Script-host parentage + ADS-shape filename + Zone.Identifier exclusion is the cleanest single-event match. Cross-checked Infosecurity Magazine for technique confirmation. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/fsbs-matryoshka-1-3-gamaredons-gifts-that-keeps-unpacking-gammaphish-and-gammaworm/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/gamaredon-worm-ntfs-data-streams/ • https://undercodenews.com/silent-infiltration-russian-linked-gamaredon-worm-exploits-windows-hidden-streams-to-haunt-ukrainian-systems-without-a-trace-video/

title: GammaWorm NTFS ADS Module Hide By Script Host
id: 9a2dde54-c81f-4773-bce4-5e8c1d0a72f6
description: Script interpreter (wscript / cscript / powershell) writes to a file path matching an NTFS Alternate Data Stream (filename:streamname), excluding Zone.Identifier — Gamaredon GammaWorm module hide.
references:
    - https://blog.sekoia.io/fsbs-matryoshka-1-3-gamaredons-gifts-that-keeps-unpacking-gammaphish-and-gammaworm/
    - https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/gamaredon-worm-ntfs-data-streams/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/02
tags:
    - attack.t1564.004
    - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:
    category: file_event
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
        TargetFilename|re: '^[A-Za-z]:\\.+\\[^:\\/]+:[^:\\/]+$'
    filter_zone:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - ':Zone.Identifier'
            - ':SmartScreen'
    condition: selection and not filter_zone
falsepositives:
    - Backup/AV products writing ADS metadata
    - Browser-downloaded files retaining Zone.Identifier (filtered)
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:15 (@Image:(*\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\WScript.exe OR *\\CScript.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe)) -@TargetFilename:*\:Zone.Identifier -@TargetFilename:*\:SmartScreen
#event_simpleName=FileWritten ContextImageFileName=/(wscript|cscript|powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i | regex(":[^:\\\\\\/]+$", field=TargetFileName) | TargetFileName!=/:Zone\.Identifier$/i | TargetFileName!=/:SmartScreen$/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Filesystem.file_name="*:*" AND NOT Filesystem.file_name IN ("*::$DATA") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Filesystem.file_name="*:*" AND NOT Filesystem.file_name IN ("*::$DATA") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime)
[LLM] GammaSteel registry-staged module fan-out — PowerShell writes many binary blobs under one key Installation Medium
Hunts GammaSteel's documented self-staging behaviour: the PowerShell-based stealer writes ~71 DPAPI-encrypted modules as binary values into a single registry key, used as its in-memory loading store. The fan-out of binary registry values from a single PowerShell process to one parent key is article-specific and very rare. Rationale: Sekoia and follow-on coverage describe GammaSteel staging 71 encrypted PowerShell modules in the registry, protected by Windows DPAPI. Threshold ≥20 distinct binary values under one HKCU/HKLM\Software key written by a single PowerShell/wscript process in 30 minutes catches the staging without over-firing on legitimate per-value config writes. Multi-event correlation, so Sigma is intentionally skipped. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/fsbs-matryoshka-1-3-gamaredons-gifts-that-keeps-unpacking-gammaphish-and-gammaworm/ • https://cyberpress.org/gamaredon-apt-hides-malware/
ATT&CKT1112 T1140 T1055.012
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
DeviceRegistryEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryValueModified") | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe") | where RegistryValueType in ("Binary","None") | where RegistryKey startswith @"HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\" or RegistryKey startswith @"HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\" | summarize DistinctValues=dcount(RegistryValueName), TotalWrites=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Sample=any(RegistryValueData) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RegistryKey, bin(Timestamp, 30m) | where DistinctValues >= 20 | order by DistinctValues desc
ImRegistryEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where EventType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryValueModified") | where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe") | where RegistryValueType in ("Binary","REG_BINARY") | summarize DistinctValues=dcount(RegistryValue), TotalWrites=count() by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, RegistryKey, bin(TimeGenerated, 30m) | where DistinctValues >= 20
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:13 (@Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\WScript.exe)) (@TargetObject:(*\\Software\\* OR *\\SOFTWARE\\*))
#event_simpleName=AsepValueUpdate ContextImageFileName=/(powershell|pwsh|wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i | regex("\\\\Software\\\\", field=RegObjectName, flags=i) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RegObjectName], function={distinct_values := count(field=RegValueName, distinct=true) | total := count()}) | distinct_values >= 20
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count as value_count dc(Registry.registry_value_name) as distinct_values values(Registry.registry_key_name) as keys from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe") AND Registry.action="modified" by Registry.dest Registry.user Registry.registry_key_name span=_time=30m | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | where distinct_values >= 20
| tstats summariesonly=false count as value_count dc(Registry.registry_value_name) as distinct_values values(Registry.registry_key_name) as keys from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe") AND Registry.action="modified" by Registry.dest Registry.user Registry.registry_key_name span=_time=30m | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | where distinct_values >= 20
[LLM] GammaSteel S3 exfiltration — script/PowerShell HTTP egress to AWS S3 bucket Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the GammaSteel exfiltration path: a script host or PowerShell process not normally seen on the wire issues an outbound HTTPS connection to *.s3.amazonaws.com (or s3.<region>.amazonaws.com) to upload harvested files. Article specifies S3 as the primary exfil with attacker-controlled web servers as a fallback. Rationale: Article explicitly names AWS S3 as GammaSteel's exfil destination with attacker-controlled fallback. The hunt isolates the unusual combination of script-host parentage and S3 egress — neither AWSPowerShell nor aws-cli are in the included process list, so legitimate S3 backup activity from a developer workstation falls outside scope. Tier set to hunting because S3 is widely used; analyst should pivot from any hit to the parent process chain. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/fsbs-matryoshka-1-3-gamaredons-gifts-that-keeps-unpacking-gammaphish-and-gammaworm/ • https://cyberpress.org/gamaredon-apt-hides-malware/
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1041

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\mshta.exe OR *\\curl.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\WScript.exe OR *\\CScript.exe)) (@DestinationHostname:(*.s3.amazonaws.com OR s3.*.amazonaws.com OR s3-*.amazonaws.com))

C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("104.194.140.6") or RemoteUrl has_any ("quitethepastry.ru", "bold.zsjtn41091.workers.dev", "iiwdsxwamylbwwsoyrmj.supabase.co", "efficiency-planes-emotions-fascinating.trycloudflare.com", "freefoodaid.com", "wellnesscaremed.com")

          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

let BadDomains = dynamic(["quitethepastry.ru", "bold.zsjtn41091.workers.dev", "iiwdsxwamylbwwsoyrmj.supabase.co", "efficiency-planes-emotions-fascinating.trycloudflare.com", "freefoodaid.com", "wellnesscaremed.com"]);

| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-8088", "CVE-2026-21509")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-8088", "CVE-2026-21509")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
